Failure to compensate for delay results in visible misalignment [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the system calculates a predicted projection deviation based on measured delay and uses this to compensate for the delay. It reports that before compensation, the average projection delay was 12.5 ms. After compensation, the mean apparent projection delay dropped to 0.147 ms. The text describes the measurement of 'angular deviation' between the rotating disk's pattern and projected markers as the metric for delay. The reduction of this deviation (misalignment) from 12.5 ms to near zero (0.147 ms) upon compensation supports the claim that failure to compensate results in visible misalignment (represented by the significant angular deviation/delay).
